title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Prompt Learning – Aparna Dhinakaran, Arize
talk_summary: Arize ran a system-prompt-learning loop on Claude Code and Cline: run the agent on SWE-bench, judge failures with an LLM-as-judge that returns English explanations, then feed those explanations plus the original prompt into a meta-prompt that emits new rules appended to CLAUDE.md/.clinerules. With only 150 training examples and no fine-tuning, they raised resolved GitHub issues by ~5% (Claude Code) and ~15% (Cline).

takeaways.what_they_do: Run the agent, run unit tests, pass problem+solution+test output to an LLM judge that returns pass/fail plus a written explanation of the failure category; feed original prompt, existing rules, and explanations into a meta-prompt that generates new rules appended to the agent's rules file.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We passed in the original claude or client system prompt... and then we passed in here was the input, here was the LM is a judge eval, and then here was the actual explanation
takeaways.numbers: 150 SWE-bench examples; +5% issues resolved (Claude Code), +15% (Cline); no fine-tuning

takeaways.technique: Judge must emit explanations, not just scores
takeaways.what_they_do: The eval prompt explicitly asks why it failed and what categories of error occurred, because the explanation is the training signal for the meta-prompt; they credit eval-prompt quality as the key differentiator vs DSPy GEPA.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We actually asked for an explanation. Why did it actually mess up?

takeaways.what_they_do: They spent most effort iterating the judge/eval prompt itself, and claim this is why their loop needed far fewer rollouts than GEPA's prompt optimizer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we spent a lot of time actually developing and iterating on the evals and the eval prompts really mattered
takeaways.numbers: GEPA 'required many many loops and rollouts' vs 'a fraction of that'

takeaways.technique: Cheap prompt learning instead of fine-tuning/RL
takeaways.what_they_do: Argue RL is sample-inefficient and data-hungry; prompt learning needs only a small labeled set and English feedback, no model changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It can be sample inefficient. It takes a lot of data to get what you want. It's time inensive. It's data hungry.

takeaways.what_they_do: Both agents expose an append-only rules file (CLAUDE.md, .clinerules) that starts empty and accumulates learned rules, keeping the base system prompt untouched.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they both kind of come with something that you can append rules to... it starts off empty
